title: Cocktail 2 Grew on Saturday When Everyone Else Crashes. Shahid's Third-Biggest Opener Has the Diaspora Pouring Again.
excerpt: Fourteen years after Deepika owned the original, Homi Adajania's vibe-franchise sequel posted a higher Day 2 than Day 1 — a rom-com curve almost nobody manages in 2026.
body:
It opened on a Friday with a love triangle, a Sicilian skyline, and fourteen years of nostalgia riding shotgun. By Sunday afternoon, Cocktail 2 had quietly done the thing every romantic comedy dreams of and almost none manage in 2026: it grew on Saturday instead of crashing.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=XXxUqLHq1xg

That is the headline, and it is a bigger deal than the raw rupees suggest. In a multiplex economy where most films front-load their entire run into opening day and then fall off a cliff, Homi Adajania's spiritual sequel posted a *higher* second day than its first — a clean upward curve that tells you word of mouth is doing the heavy lifting.

https://x.com/SubhashK_Jha/status/2068013657070702831

> "I expect comparisons will come, but the good thing is — this isn't a sequel, it's a franchise. It's a vibe franchise, and the characters are distinct." — Kriti Sanon, on stepping into a world Deepika Padukone once owned

The numbers, poured neat

> "Critical reception has been mixed, the kind of "fun but familiar" verdict that usually softens a film's legs."

The film took a confident ₹13.10 crore net on its opening Friday in India, then jumped roughly 25 percent to ₹16.39 crore on Saturday as evening shows filled out across urban centres. Sunday was tracking live through the afternoon, with trade sites projecting an opening weekend comfortably in the ₹32–35 crore band domestically, and a worldwide gross already nudging the ₹50 crore mark inside two days.

For context, that opening day didn't just clear the bar — it stepped over some legends. Cocktail 2's Friday outpaced the first-day numbers of the original Cocktail (₹10.95 crore back in 2012), Alia and Arjun's 2 States (₹12.40 crore), and Humpty Sharma Ki Dulhania (₹9.05 crore). The decade's benchmark, *Yeh Jawaani Hai Deewani* at ₹19.45 crore, still sits on its throne — but in the modern urban rom-com bracket, this is genuinely one of the strongest starts in years.

It is also a personal milestone for the leads. The opening hands Shahid Kapoor his third-biggest debut ever, a meaningful rebound after his February release *O Romeo* fizzled at ₹8.50 crore on day one. And for Kriti Sanon, it's now her second-highest post-pandemic opener, behind only *Crew*.

A sequel that isn't one

Here's the sleight of hand the makers pulled off. The 2012 original — Saif Ali Khan caught between Deepika Padukone's magnetic, self-destructing Veronica and Diana Penty's wide-eyed Meera — is a sacred text for a certain generation of NRIs who watched it on loop in their first London or New Jersey apartments. Touching it was always going to be a risk.

So they didn't. Cocktail 2 keeps the title, the Pritam-scored sun-drenched mood, and the messy three-way chemistry, but swaps in an entirely new trio: Shahid, Kriti, and Rashmika Mandanna, with Sanjay Dutt rounding out the ensemble. Shot largely in Sicily, it trades London grey for Mediterranean gold — and judging by the Saturday bump, audiences are buying the postcard.

Critical reception has been mixed, the kind of "fun but familiar" verdict that usually softens a film's legs. That the weekend held up anyway says the audience came for the vibe, not the reviews — exactly the franchise logic Kriti described.

Why the diaspora cares

This is the part that matters if you're reading from Edison or Hounslow or Brampton. Cocktail 2 went out worldwide on June 19, and the overseas number is already healthy — roughly $1 million grossed abroad in the first stretch, a strong sign for a non-event rom-com with no franchise spectacle to sell.

For NRI audiences, the original Cocktail is comfort food, and the sequel is currently playing in theatres across the US, UK, and Canada — check AMC, Cinemark, Cineworld and your local desi multiplex, where the Friday-to-Sunday shows tend to sell hardest. No streaming date has been announced yet; given the theatrical legs, expect the makers to milk the big screen for a few weeks before any OTT window opens.

What's next

The real test arrives Monday, when the weekend cushion disappears and the working-week trickle begins — and then again on June 26, when *Welcome to the Jungle* and Jr NTR's *Dragon* crash into the same screens and the fight for showtimes turns ugly. A film that grows on Saturday has the kind of momentum that survives a crowded calendar. Cocktail 2 has poured a strong first round. Now we find out if the buzz lasts past the hangover.
